 As the global energy transition accelerates, unprecedented volumes of fluids are being injected into and extracted from the subsurface, spanning gigatonne-scale CO₂ storage, enhanced geothermal systems (EGS), compressed air and hydrogen storage, and large-scale wastewater disposal. These operations impose complex thermo-hydro-mechanical (THM) perturbations on geological formations, altering pore pressure fields, effective stress states, and thermal gradients across spatial scales ranging from pore throats to sedimentary basins. The coupled THM processes governing fault reactivation, fracture propagation, and induced seismicity remain insufficiently understood, particularly at the scales and durations demanded by climate-relevant deployment targets.
 This minisymposium brings together experimentalists, modelers, and field scientists to address the porous media physics underlying injection-induced and extraction-triggered seismicity in real-world subsurface energy and storage operations. We welcome contributions across scales, from coupling mechanisms at the pore-scale to geomechanical responses at the reservoir-to-basin-scale, with emphasis on predictive capabilities needed for safe, large-scale subsurface operations.
